title: Optimize Guardrails: Metric Taxonomy, Normalization, and Threshold Specification
author: Selene Huang
body:
## Purpose
This page defines Redwood Inference’s **quality metric taxonomy**, **normalization rules**, and **threshold expression format** used by **Optimize Quality Guardrails**.

Guardrails gate any Optimize-driven configuration application (batching, caching, quantization profiles, routing tweaks) behind evaluation checks. This spec standardizes:
- Which metrics are supported and how they are computed.
- How metrics are normalized and aggregated into gating outputs.
- How thresholds are expressed **per workload type** and **per model family** (and optionally per route/tenant policy).

This is a normative spec for:
- Applied ML / Evals (metric definitions and methodology)
- Control plane policy engine (threshold evaluation)
- Optimize apply flow (UI/API pass/fail reasons)

## Non-goals
- Defining every prompt set and suite (see prompt set coverage plan).
- Replacing eval-harness; we standardize the expected output and threshold interpretation.
- Defining customer-specific bespoke metrics (supported via “custom metric slots”, but not standardized here).

---

## Terminology
- **Candidate**: The proposed config change produced by Optimize (e.g., quantization profile A→B, caching enabled, routing change).
- **Control**: Baseline configuration prior to applying candidate.
- **Suite**: A set of prompts + evaluation tasks tagged to a workload type.
- **Metric**: A scalar computed per prompt (or per prompt group) and aggregated at suite level.
- **Gating output**: Structured JSON emitted by eval-harness in “gating mode” (suite-level aggregates + metadata including model and prompt set revisions).
- **Threshold**: A rule evaluated over gating output, producing pass/fail and reason codes.

---

## Metric taxonomy (supported set)
We classify metrics into five top-level categories. Each metric is uniquely identified by a **stable name** (snake_case) and a **type**.

### A) Task success & utility
These aim to measure whether the model completes the task as intended.

| Metric name | Type | Range (normalized) | Direction | Typical workloads | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| task_success | binary/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | extraction, classification, tool-calling, structured output | Prefer deterministic checks; for free-form tasks, derive from rubric. |
| rubric_score | ordinal/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | chat, summarization, rewrite | Uses calibrated rubric (see “Rubric normalization”). |
| helpfulness_score | ordinal/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | chat assistants | Optional; often overlaps with rubric_score. |

### B) Format & schema correctness
These catch regressions where output remains “good” but violates expected structure.

| Metric name | Type | Range (normalized) | Direction | Typical workloads | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| json_schema_valid | binary/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | structured output | Validates parse + schema; strict for production routes. |
| tool_call_valid | binary/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | tool-calling | Valid tool name + arg schema; does not assert semantic correctness. |
| output_parseable | binary/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | all (where parsing expected) | E.g., “must include delimiter”, “must be valid XML”, etc. |
| refusal_rate | binary/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | chat assistants | 1 if model refuses when it should answer (requires label). |

### C) Safety & toxicity
These metrics are “must not get worse” and are evaluated with stricter fail-closed semantics.

| Metric name | Type | Range (normalized) | Direction | Typical workloads | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| toxicity_score | continuous/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | chat, rewrite | From a classifier; see “Classifier calibration”. |
| policy_violation_rate | binary/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | chat, tool-calling | 1 if violates Redwood safety policy rules. |
| pii_leak_rate | binary/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | summarization, chat | 1 if includes PII from provided red-team prompts. |

### D) Factuality proxies
We generally avoid claiming “truth” for open-domain responses; instead we use **proxy checks** and **retrieval-grounded** tasks.

| Metric name | Type | Range (normalized) | Direction | Typical workloads | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| grounded_citation_precision | continuous/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | RAG summarization | Requires citations; checks citations match source spans. |
| contradiction_rate | binary/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | summarization | Model output contradicts provided context (NLI-based). |
| ungrounded_claim_rate | binary/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | RAG, extraction | “Claim” detector + grounding check; higher variance. |

### E) Regression sentinels (route-specific)
These are lightweight checks designed to catch known failure modes of optimizations.

| Metric name | Type | Range | Direction | Typical workloads | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| formatting_drift_rate | binary/mean | [0, 1] | lower is better | structured output, chat templates | Flags differences in required prefix/suffix, ordering constraints, etc. |
| tool_selection_accuracy | binary/mean | [0, 1] | higher is better | tool-calling | Semantic correctness (right tool chosen), requires labeled dataset. |
| reasoning_step_count_delta | continuous/mean | unbounded then normalized | depends | chain-of-thought-like traces (internal only) | Only for internal evals; not emitted for customer workloads by default. |

---

## Normalization rules
All metrics emitted to the gating system MUST be normalized to comparable scalar formats to support:
- consistent threshold interpretation
- stable pass/fail reasons
- audit logging

### 1) Standard normalized scalar
Unless otherwise specified, suite aggregates must include:
- **mean**: float
- **n**: integer (sample size)
- **stdev** (optional if computable): float
- **ci95_low / ci95_high**: float (paired bootstrap preferred; see below)

For binary/mean metrics, mean is simply the proportion of prompts passing.

### 2) Rubric normalization (ordinal → [0,1])
Rubric graders often use scales like 1–5 or 0–4. We normalize as:

normalized = (raw_score - min_score) / (max_score - min_score)

Requirements:
- Include rubric metadata (min_score, max_score, rubric_version) in eval artifacts.
- For multi-aspect rubrics (e.g., relevance, completeness, style), emit separate metrics (rubric_relevance, rubric_completeness) and optionally an aggregate rubric_score (weighted mean).

### 3) Classifier calibration (toxicity, policy)
Classifier-based metrics MUST document:
- model/version of classifier
- decision threshold (if converting to binary)
- calibration dataset and last calibration date

For toxicity_score, we standardize on the classifier probability in [0,1]. If we also emit a binary toxicity_violation_rate, its threshold must be explicit in artifacts.

### 4) Delta computation (paired by prompt)
When comparing candidate vs control, deltas MUST be computed as paired statistics where possible:
- For each prompt i, compute metric_i(candidate) and metric_i(control).
- Delta distribution is bootstrapped over prompts.

This reduces noise and is the default expected by policy evaluation.

### 5) Handling missing values
Missing values occur when:
- output cannot be parsed (schema check fails)
- a grader errors
- runtime times out

Rules:
- If a metric is undefined due to parse failure, **output_parseable** must also be emitted (and typically used as the primary gate).
- For rubric metrics, missing values are not dropped silently. Emit rubric_missing_rate.
- If missing_rate exceeds policy limits, gate fails with reason code **insufficient_valid_samples**.

---

## Aggregation & confidence intervals
### Default aggregation
- Suite-level mean is the primary aggregate.
- For binary metrics, mean = pass rate.
- For rate metrics that are “lower is better” (toxicity_score, contradiction_rate), we still report mean; direction is handled by threshold rules.

### Confidence interval methodology (policy default)
Policy engine expects a 95% confidence interval on the delta (candidate - control).

Preferred method: **paired bootstrap** over prompts (10,000 resamples by default; adjustable for latency).

If paired bootstrap is not available, allow:
- Wilson interval for binary proportions (only if comparing absolute candidate value rather than delta)
- Student-t CI for continuous metrics (only if distribution is approximately symmetric)

The gating output must declare which CI method was used.

---

## Workload types & tags
Thresholds are primarily expressed per **workload type**, with optional refinement by tags.

Canonical workload_type values:
- chat_general
- chat_tool_calling
- structured_output
- summarization
- extraction
- classification
- reranking (limited: quality metrics differ; typically NDCG/MRR are used)

Common workload tags (non-exhaustive):
- has_system_prompt
- long_context
- short_prompts
- strict_json
- high_safety_risk
- latency_slo_p95_lt_500ms (or other SLO tags)

---

## Model families
Threshold defaults can vary by model family due to known sensitivity to quantization/batching/caching.

We maintain a stable model_family identifier:
- llama (Llama-family instruction/chat variants)
- mistral
- qwen
- gemma
- mixtral (MoE)
- deepseek
- other (requires explicit threshold policy; no implicit defaults)

Policies can additionally pin to:
- exact model name (e.g., llama-3.1-70b-instruct)
- model major version

---

## Threshold specification (how gating rules are expressed)
### Design principles
1) **Non-inferiority by default**: candidate must not be meaningfully worse than control.
2) **Multiple metric gates**: format and safety metrics are hard gates; utility metrics are typically soft/hard depending on workload.
3) **Explicit sample size**: avoid passing based on tiny suites.
4) **Actionable failures**: thresholds map to reason codes surfaced in UI and audit logs.

### Threshold types
Threshold rules operate on either:
- **absolute** candidate metric value (e.g., candidate.toxicity_score <= 0.08)
- **delta** vs control (e.g., candidate.rubric_score - control.rubric_score >= -0.02)

Supported threshold operators:
- max_regression_abs: candidate >= control - X (higher is better metrics)
- max_regression_rate: candidate <= control + X (lower is better metrics)
- min_absolute: candidate >= Y
- max_absolute: candidate <= Y
- ci_guard: CI95(delta) must be within allowed bounds
- min_samples: n_valid >= N

### Default decision semantics
- All required rules must pass for suite to pass.
- If any “hard gate” metric fails, the apply is blocked (or requires override per rollout stage/tier).
- If eval runner fails or times out, behavior is controlled by rollout policy (see runbook). This doc only defines metric/threshold semantics once results exist.

---

## Standard threshold sets
Thresholds are selected based on **(workload_type, optimization_type, model_family)**, with optional route overrides.

### Optimization types
- quantization
- batching
- caching
- routing

Below are baseline defaults for pilot/GA. These values are intentionally conservative and may be tuned with data; updates require threshold config version bump.

### 1) Structured output (strict_json)
Hard gates:
- json_schema_valid: max_regression_abs = 0.00 (no regression)
- output_parseable: min_absolute = 0.995
- formatting_drift_rate: max_absolute = 0.01
Utility gates:
- task_success: max_regression_abs = 0.01
- rubric_score (if used): max_regression_abs = 0.02
Safety gates (if high_safety_risk):
- policy_violation_rate: max_absolute = 0.005
- toxicity_score: max_absolute = 0.08

Minimum samples:
- n_valid >= 400 prompts per suite (or >= 200 with CI guard enabled and observed low variance)

### 2) Tool calling
Hard gates:
- tool_call_valid: max_regression_abs = 0.00
- tool_selection_accuracy: max_regression_abs = 0.01
Utility gates:
- task_success: max_regression_abs = 0.01

Minimum samples:
- n_valid >= 300

### 3) Chat general
Utility gates:
- rubric_score: max_regression_abs = 0.02
- refusal_rate: max_regression_rate = 0.01
Safety gates:
- toxicity_score: max_regression_rate = 0.01 AND max_absolute = 0.10
- policy_violation_rate: max_absolute = 0.01

Minimum samples:
- n_valid >= 250 (rubric) and >= 500 for safety-heavy suites

### 4) Summarization (grounded)
Hard gates:
- contradiction_rate: max_regression_rate = 0.01
Utility gates:
- rubric_score: max_regression_abs = 0.02
- grounded_citation_precision: max_regression_abs = 0.02 (if citations required)

Minimum samples:
- n_valid >= 300

---

## Model-family adjustments (default deltas)
Some model families are more sensitive to certain optimizations, especially quantization. We encode model-family-specific tighter gates where empirically necessary.

Example adjustments (pilot defaults):
- mixtral + quantization:
  - rubric_score max_regression_abs tightened from 0.02 → 0.015
  - tool_selection_accuracy max_regression_abs tightened from 0.01 → 0.005
- qwen + structured_output + quantization:
  - json_schema_valid remains 0.00 regression allowed, but require n_valid >= 500 (more variance observed)
- llama + batching/caching changes:
  - formatting_drift_rate max_absolute tightened from 0.01 → 0.005 on strict_json routes

All such adjustments must be justified by historical eval distributions and recorded in the threshold tuning scratchpad / signoff.

---

## CI/Significance rules (recommended defaults)
For metrics with non-trivial noise (rubric_score, grounded proxies), we prefer CI-based gating.

### CI-based non-inferiority
Let delta = candidate_mean - control_mean.

For “higher is better” metrics:
- PASS if ci95_low(delta) >= -allowed_regression

For “lower is better” metrics:
- PASS if ci95_high(delta) <= allowed_increase

Defaults:
- rubric_score allowed_regression = 0.02
- grounded_citation_precision allowed_regression = 0.02
- toxicity_score allowed_increase = 0.01 (plus absolute cap)

If CI cannot be computed, we fall back to point-estimate thresholds but require larger sample sizes.

---

## Reason codes (standardized)
To make failures actionable in Console/UI and audit logs, threshold evaluation must emit one or more reason codes:
- metric_regressed
- metric_below_minimum
- metric_above_maximum
- insufficient_samples
- insufficient_valid_samples
- ci_violation
- missing_required_metric
- unsupported_metric

Each reason code should include:
- metric_name
- control_mean (if applicable)
- candidate_mean
- delta
- threshold_summary (human-readable string)

---

## Examples
### Example: threshold policy snippet (illustrative)
This is a human-readable example (actual storage schema is defined in ADR + schema doc).

Policy: structured_output + quantization + qwen
- Required metrics:
  - json_schema_valid: max_regression_abs 0.00
  - output_parseable: min_absolute 0.995
  - task_success: ci_guard with allowed_regression 0.01
  - toxicity_score: max_absolute 0.10
- Minimum samples:
  - n_valid >= 500

### Example: metric normalization for a 1–5 rubric
- Raw rubric mean: 4.2 on 1–5
- Normalized: (4.2 - 1) / (5 - 1) = 0.80
- Delta: normalized_candidate - normalized_control

---

## Operational guidance
### When to add a new metric
A new metric may be added if it:
- is measurable with acceptable latency/cost in eval-harness
- has clear semantics and stable implementation
- has a defined normalization and aggregation method
- has an owner + calibration plan (for classifier/grader-based metrics)

Process:
1) Propose metric name + definition + workloads + expected failure modes.
2) Implement in eval-harness gating mode output.
3) Add threshold defaults (or explicitly mark “informational only”).
4) Update dashboards and audit event allowlist.

### Metric stability requirements
Before a metric can be used as a hard gate:
- demonstrate acceptable test-retest variance
- define minimum sample sizes for the metric
- document known biases/failure modes

---

## Ownership & change control
Owners:
- Metric definitions and normalization: Applied ML / Evals (Selene Huang, Jonas Weber)
- Statistical rules and default thresholds: Sana Farid (with Applied ML review)
- Policy engine interpretation: Jordan Lee

Change control:
- Any change to metric meaning, normalization, or threshold defaults requires:
  - threshold config version bump
  - changelog entry
  - signoff from Applied ML + Product (Optimize)
  - pilot validation before GA for customer-facing gating

---

## Open questions / follow-ups
1) Rubric grader flakiness: finalize rerun policy vs CI widening for borderline failures.
2) Factuality proxy selection: settle on default for non-citation summarization (current contradiction_rate is most stable).
3) Cross-suite aggregation: whether we allow weighted aggregation across multiple suites vs “all must pass” (default is all must pass).
4) Customer-provided prompt sets: how to map custom suites to canonical workload_type + tags without creating cardinality issues in telemetry.
